data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive 'rule of action' based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness) rather than probability; we prefer the theory that has withstood the severest tests because it is currently the best approximation to truth, not because we predict it will survive future tests.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper explicitly equates acting on a theory with assigning it a higher probability of future success.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the concept of verisimilitude cannot be defined without relying on inductive assumptions about the structure of the world.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Differentiation between logical probability (which remains zero for universal laws) and verisimilitude (closeness to truth). Corroboration reports the severity of tests passed, acting as a marker for high verisimilitude.
